en: Preface to the *Ten Regulations on the Dharma-Eye Chan Master*:

The principles and intent of our school cannot be opened up by means of a single [text] alone. For this reason, both Buddhas and patriarchs have each composed treatises; thus they established the fundamental tenets to meet the diverse capacities of sentient beings.
The Great Master Fayan, beginning with his intimate realization of the unknowable, trod the Way without error; his proclamation of the Way reached its ultimate height.
Yet, at that time, the world’s encounter with this true Dharma gradually declined, and the grand paradigm of the Patriarchs and Buddhas could not be transmitted forever.
Troubled by the frequent confusion and turmoil caused by the chaff of this turbid age, he composed the *Ten Regulations* (*Shiguilun*) to recount the reality of the former patriarchs.
It addresses the defects of the time; it may truly be said that its righteousness is correct, its principles profound, and its expression eloquent.

How can one not regret having this work yet remaining unaware of it, or knowing it yet failing to put it into practice? This spring, the community of Jixiang Chan Monastery in the Eastern Capital inquired into and deliberated upon this matter.
Each of the Chan practitioners, with a resolute will born of indignation and earnest desire, sought to publish it in woodblocks, and thus they made this request.

I have composed this preface. Unable to bear the joy of obtaining the pearl from the red water, I have briefly set forth these humble words merely to express my sense of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). At that time.
On the occasion of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa Assembly in the year of Xinsi (the eleventh year of the Baoli era), [the author] stayed at Wanshantang beneath the Candana grove;
there, burning incense and prostrating a hundred times, he wrote this preface to the *Ten Regulations for the Chan School*. *Inzhuyue* (Seal of the Finger-Moon).
Wenyi was liberated from the heavy shackles of worldly life in his youth and heard the essential teachings of the Dharma as he grew up. He traveled to visit various masters for nearly thirty years;
moreover, the ancestral lineages were vast and expansive, with the Southern School being the most flourishing. Yet, among those who had attained realization therein, such individuals were rare.

Nevertheless, although the principle is realized all at once, its realization must be verified through gradual stages. Thus, while the methods for establishing the school and transforming beings are manifold, their ultimate aim is to benefit sentient beings by guiding them.

In a single debate, if one has not yet undergone the process of instruction and discussion, it is difficult to shatter habitual perceptions and attachments. One may drive right view onto a deviant path and drown the Great Meaning in heterodox doctrines.

Thus, later students are misled and unjustly cast into the cycle of *saṃsāra*. Wen Yi’s [Zhizheng] profound understanding of the Middle Way was such that his efforts to refute [false views] could not reach them;
though his resolve to block their tracks was vigorous, his wisdom was no match for the "mole-rat" of the river. Thus, he forcibly attempted to manifest [the truth] within the realm of the ineffable.

These words state: Within the midst of non-existence, one forcibly maintains the existence of dharmas. This treatise, "Pointing Out Illnesses in the Lineage School," consists of ten sections for the purpose of discerning and clarifying various false statements, thereby remedying the corruptions of the present age. I have respectfully composed this preface.
The Ten Regulations of Chan Master Fayan: The Sequential Order of the Text.
First: To falsely act as a teacher for others when one’s own mind-ground is not yet enlightened.
First, they protect the traditions of their school and do not allow for open discussion.
Second, they merely uphold the formal instructions and do not understand the underlying vital principle.
Third, they fail to observe the appropriate timing in their responses and lack the "eye of the lineage. Fourth, [they fail to grasp the essential meaning].
Fifth, the contradiction between principle and phenomena, failing to distinguish between the tainted and the pure;
sixth, arbitrary judgments regarding ancient and modern sayings without having undergone refinement;
seventh, the mere rote memorization of manifest proclamations, lacking the wondrous function of spontaneous understanding when the occasion arises.
Eighth, not being conversant with the scriptural teachings, they cite proofs from them in a confused manner;
ninth, having no concern for phonology and prosody and lacking mastery of the principles of the Way, they delight in composing songs and verses;
tenth, protecting their own shortcomings, they delight in contending for victory and defeat.跋 (Colophon)
**Treatise on the Ten Regulations of the Chan School by Chan Master Jinghui Fayen** **Discourse One:
On Taking the Role of Teacher for Others When One’s Own Mind-Ground is Not Yet Clarified** It is said:
The Dharma-gate of the mind-ground is the very foundation of study and practice. What, then, is the mind-ground? It is as the Tathāgata...
This is the nature of Great Enlightenment. Since beginningless time, due to a single moment of inversion, one has mistaken external objects for the self.
Greed and desire blaze fiercely as one wanders through birth and death; awakening and illumination are obscured, shrouded by ignorance, and driven by the wheel of karma without freedom.
Once one loses this human body, it is difficult to return for long kalpas. For this reason, when the Buddhas appear in the world, they provide many gates of skillful means.

Yet those who linger on words and seek meaning in phrases fall back into the extremes of eternalism or nihilism. The Patriarchs, out of compassion, transmitted the Mind-Seal alone, so that one need not pass through successive stages but may suddenly transcend both the ordinary and the sagely.
They intended only for one to awaken for oneself and forever sever the root of doubt. Those of recent times have mostly been arrogant and negligent toward the monastic community.
Though they enter the forest [of the sangha], they are indolent in their aspiration for inquiry; even if they do apply their minds, they fail to choose a true master.

Through the errors of false teachers, they lose their sense of direction together. Without having understood the nature of the faculties and objects, they hastily form perverse interpretations and enter the realm of Māra, utterly losing the correct cause.

They know only the urgent task of maintaining the institution and falsely claim the title of "spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra). They value empty fame in the world, caring not at all for the succession of evil.
This not only blinds and deafens future generations, but also causes the social and moral teachings to decay and fall into ruin.

Ascending the high and vast throne of the Dharma King, one would rather lie upon an iron bed; enduring the final reproach of Cunda, one might suddenly drink molten copper. One must tremble with great fear;
it is not appropriate to remain complacent. The transgression of slandering the Mahāyāna is no small retribution.
The second discourse concerns the partisan protection of one's school’s traditions that blocks open discussion.

It says: When the Patriarch came from the West, it was not because there was a dharma to be transmitted; rather, he directly pointed to the human mind so that one might see one's nature and become a Buddha.
How could there be any "school traditions" (men-feng) to be held in high esteem? Nevertheless, later generations of masters established their transformative teachings.

There were differences that led to successive developments and adaptations. For instance, although the two masters Huineng and Shenxiu originally shared the same patriarchal lineage, their views diverged;
consequently, the world referred to them as the Southern School and the Northern School. After Huineng had passed away, the two masters Shenhui and Puji succeeded him in propagating the teachings.
Sishi succeeded Xianshi, and Rang succeeded Mazu; there was also the one known as Shitou of Jiangxi.

From these two branches, various lineages were divided and established, each presiding over a particular region. Their origins and transmissions began like the first trickle of a stream and cannot be fully recorded.

Reaching the times of Deshan, Linji, Weiyang, Caodong, Xuefeng, Yunmen, and others, each had their own distinct teaching methods and pedagogical arrangements, categorized by their relative heights and qualities.

As for the successive generations of descendants who protect their ancestral lineage, they fail to trace back to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), ultimately branching out into many divergent paths.

They attack one another like a sword and a shield, such that neither the monastics (*kṛṣṇa*) nor the laity (*avadāta*) can distinguish the truth. Alas! They do not realize that the Great Way has no fixed direction and that the flow of the Dharma shares a single flavor.
To apply colors toward the void, to thrust a needle into iron and stone, to vie for victory through supernatural powers, and to display eloquence as if practicing samādhi—
whereupon the blades of right and wrong arise and the mountains of self and other grow high— such anger is precisely the view and understanding of an asura.
In the end, they become followers of external paths. Had they not encountered a virtuous friend, it would have been difficult to extricate them from the ford of delusion.
Although this was a wholesome cause, it invited an evil result.
To raise up and grasp the main principles while remaining ignorant of the underlying lineage—this is the third [point].
The Commentary states: Now, those who wish to proclaim the primary vehicle (zōngshèng) and uphold the essential principles of the Dharma must understand the bloodline (xuèmài);
otherwise, they are all falsely claiming to be heterodox. Among them, some may first proclaim and later uphold [the teaching], modulating the doctrine and employing sharp, decisive thrusts.

When the Patriarchal Command is applied, life and death rest in their hands. At times they stand like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, impenetrable as water; at other times they temporarily grant permission and let go.

Acting according to the waves and following the currents, like a king brandishing his sword, one prizes the attainment of freedom. Functioning according to the occasion, the powers of bestowal and withdrawal remain under one's own command.
Surging like waves and standing firm as mountains, swift as lightning and rushing as the wind—this is the roaming of the Great Elephant King and the true lion’s roar.
Yet I see many who fail to gauge their own strength, merely pilfering the words of others; they know only how to let go, but not how to gather in, even though they possess...
Born into this world yet devoid of the capacity for discernment, they fail to distinguish between master and servant or true and false. They defile the ancients and bury the essential tenets.
Everyone speculates beneath the faculty of thought; each and every one seeks within the realms of the five aggregates.

Thus, being ignorant of the *bodhi* that meets the eye at every turn, they achieve nothing more than a semblance of *prajñā*. To establish the banner of the Dharma upon the groundless foundation—this is to act on their behalf.

The Buddha’s proclamation is by no means an easy matter. Have you not seen how Master Yunmen said, "Throughout the entire land of the Great Tang, it is difficult to find even a single person who can raise a koan"?
Nor have you seen how Master Huangbo said, "Master Mazu produced more than eighty enlightened teachers;
when questioned, each of them was completely at a loss, with the sole exception of Master Huairang of Mount Lu."
It is still slightly lacking. One should know that at this stage, if one can understand how to raise [the koan] and uphold the guiding principles, one is already a fully accomplished master.
How do we know this? Have you not seen the ancients say: "Discern the field from the sprout; recognize the person through their words"?
Even if one were to blink an eye or raise an eyebrow, one would have already been verified at that moment; how much more so when acting as a model for others—how could one not be cautious?
The Fourth Treatise states: In responding to questions, one must not fail to observe the proper timing, nor lack the "eye of the thesis" (*siddhānta*).

Generally, one who acts as a master of the thesis must first distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. Once the heterodox and the orthodox have been distinguished, it is further essential that the timing be clearly defined.
Furthermore, one’s speech must carry the eye of the fundamental principle (*zongyan*), so that in the exchange of sharp wits, each does not fail the other.

Although there is no private agenda within the phrases, one must nevertheless discern the mark through the words. In the Cao-Dong school, striking and singing are employed as function; in the Linji school, mutual interchange constitutes the pivotal mechanism.
In the case of Shao Yang, the container and its lid meet and the stream is cut off; in the case of Wei Yang, squareness and roundness are intuitively realized.

Like a valley responding to a tone, or like a seal and its impression fitting together, although they differ in their formal protocols, there is no obstruction to their harmonious integration. Yet, recent masters have lost their foundation.

These scholars lack any basis for verification. They employ the self and others to compete for supremacy and take birth-and-death as their attainment. Where is the mind that engages with sentient beings?
Their wisdom to refute heterodoxy is unheard of. They bestow blows and shouts at random, yet claim to be the successors of Linji, Caoshan, and Deshan.

They merely say that they have profoundly penetrated the teachings of Miaoshan and Yangshan; yet, since their responses do not distinguish the fundamental principles, how could their actions reveal the essential eye?
To mock the common folk and deceive the sages and worthies is truly a cause for derision among those who observe from the sidelines.
Furthermore, they invite censure through their present retribution. Thus, Yixiu Jue said: "If you wish not to incur karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma.
As for such individuals, they are beyond reproach; having merely shed their lineage of teachers, they utterly lack personal insight.
Having no fundamental basis to rely upon, their karmic consciousness is vast and茫然 (vastly bewildered). They are only to be pitied and cannot be expected to provide a response.
The Fifth Treatise on the Non-separation of Principle and Phenomena and the Distinction between Touching and Purity states:
Generally speaking, the school of the Patriarchs and Buddhas possesses both principle and phenomena. Phenomena are established based upon principle, and principle is made manifest through phenomena.
Principle and phenomena support one another, just like eyes and feet. If there is phenomenon but no principle, one becomes mired in stagnation and cannot pass through;
if there is principle but no phenomenon, one drifts aimlessly without a point of return. To desire that these two are not dualistic, one must value their perfect integration (*yuánróng*).

Furthermore, take for example the tradition of the Caodong school: there is the biased and the correct, and there is the luminous and the dark. In the Linji school, there is the host and the guest, and there is...
The essence possesses function; yet, while the modes of manifestation differ, they are interconnected through their vital lineage, leaving nothing uncomprised and gathering all within every movement.
It is like the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*, which fully discusses both principle and phenomena, severing the duality of form and emptiness; the nature of the ocean is boundless.

All is gathered within the tip of a single hair; Mount Sumeru, though vast, is contained within a mustard seed. Thus, it is not brought about by the measures of the sages, but is the natural convergence of true principle.
Furthermore, this is not a manifestation of supernatural powers, nor is it a matter of birth or reputation; it does not depend on seeking elsewhere.

Everything is created by the mind. Since Buddhas and sentient beings are endowed with equality, if one fails to understand this essential principle and engages in groundless discourse, it will lead to a failure to distinguish between the defiled and the pure, and an inability to discern the clamor of delusion.
One becomes stuck in the confusion of the partial and the whole, and the essence and its function become muddled within the natural state.
This is called the failure to clarify a single dharma; a speck of dust obscures the eye. Unable to eradicate one's own afflictions, one remains ill.
His illness is urgent; how can it be treated? One must exercise great caution and deliberation, for this is certainly no small matter.
The sixth discourse, titled "Hasty Judgments Based on Unexamined Antiquities and Modern Sayings," states:

Now, for one who has entered the monastic community as a seeker of the Way, they must first select a virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and subsequently [rely upon] their kinsmen and friends.
Friends and acquaintances are essential for pointing the way; companions are valued for their mutual refinement through criticism and instruction.

If one merely desires to perfect oneself alone, how can one inspire the advancement of later students, uphold and propagate the religious teachings, and engage with others to benefit all living beings? What is the purpose of such an endeavor?

Observe the former masters who acted as bridges and rafts across mountains and seas, undaunted by life or death, for the sake of even a single or two transformative causes and conditions. If there were even the slightest flaw...

Regarding these matters of doubt, one must rely upon decisive discernment; it is essential to achieve clarity, establishing a standard for distinguishing the authentic from the counterfeit and serving as eyes for both humans and devas.
Only then may one loftily uphold the seal of the school and widely disseminate the true wind, citing the right and wrong of former generations and resolving uncompleted koans.
If one fails to undergo such refinement and instead makes arbitrary judgments based on antiquity and modernity, how is this any different from one who has not yet learned to wield a sword?

Yet you insist on brandishing the Great Ape (Ta’a) sword; unpracticed in the perilous passage of the *Kan* hexagram, you recklessly rely upon it to wade through the deep. Will you not suffer the calamity of wounded hands and submerged feet?
Indeed, one who excels at extracting [the essence] is like the king of geese selecting milk from water; one who does not excel at extracting is like the divine tortoise feigning its tracks.

Moreover, within these matters there are occasions of opposition and compliance, and expressions of mutual interplay; one may emerge from the realm of life yet retreat to the ground of death, or take that which is living and instead entrust it to a partial gate.
It is not permissible to indulge such a reckless mind and presume to fathom the intentions of the Sages.

How much more so regarding the essentials of the Dharma-gate of a single word, which possesses ten thousand methods for establishing transformation! One cannot but be cautious to prevent future lapses.
This concludes the seventh [section]: "Memorizing and Reciting the Manifesto Without Understanding Its Sublime Function When the Occasion Arises."
The Treatise says: One who studies Prajñā is not without the Dharma of the Teacher. Once the Dharma of the Teacher has been attained, it is essential for its great function to manifest before one;

only then does there arise even a slight degree of intimate realization. If one merely adheres strictly to the Teacher’s school, memorizing and reciting formal expositions, none of this constitutes true awakening.
All of this belongs to seeing and knowing. Thus, the ancients said: "If your vision is equal to that of your teacher, you fall short of his virtue by half;
only when your vision surpasses that of your teacher do you truly propagate his teaching. Furthermore, the Sixth Patriarch said to the Venerable Ming:
"What I have spoken with you is not a secret matter; the secret lies within you. Again, Yantou said to Xuefeng: "Every single thing flows from within one's own breast."

Thus it is known that words, staff-blows, and shouts do not depend on formal lineage transmission; their wondrous function is free and all-pervasive—how could one seek to conform them to anything else?

To disparage them is to cause pearls and gold to lose their luster; to appreciate them is to make even shards and rubble shine with brilliance. Act when it is appropriate to act, cultivating both principle and phenomena together;

employ them when it is appropriate to employ them, without the slightest deviation. This is the stuff of a true man’s character, not the business of children. One must strictly avoid following [such teachings] blindly.
To be hindered by words and phrases, and to take the mere movement of the lips and the flapping of the mouth as "sublime understanding," is to mistake the very spirit of the tradition.

How much more so when this [Dharma] does not rely on the trap or the snare to gain entry, nor can it be known through discursive thought? Its wisdom emerges from the vast and boundless realm; its spirit meets with the unfathomable state.
It is the trampling of dragons and elephants—something a donkey cannot endure.
The eighth point, "Failing to Master the Scriptural Teachings and Confusingly Citing Evidence," states:
Whenever one wishes to exalt the vehicle of our own school and cite scriptural teachings as evidence, one must first clarify the Buddha’s intent and subsequently accord with the patriarchs’ minds;
only then may one cite and practice them, weighing their relative depth and density. If, however, one fails to understand the underlying principles, one should simply...

One must strictly maintain the traditional gate-keeping of our school. Should one recklessly attempt to cite scriptural evidence, one will only incur derision. Furthermore, the *Sūtra* (Skt. *sūtra*) is the secret treasury that exhaustively points out the tracks;

the Perfect and Sudden Supreme Vehicle is entirely identical in its headings and titles. Even if one were to understand hundreds of thousands of samādhis and dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it would only increase one's own toil and have no bearing on the matter at hand.
How much more so when one realizes that provisional teachings return to the ultimate reality, thereby subsuming all branches and descendants.

Returning to the source, within the realm of true purity, not even a single speck of dust is admitted; how much less could one fail to relinquish a single dharma within the gateway of Buddha-activities?

Yet, to avoid being caught by the facts of one’s own emotional attachments and to attempt to resolve the confusion by resorting to the essence [of reality] is entirely unrelated to my ancestral patriarchs.

There are indeed many great masters who have traversed the classics and true lineages of antiquity, boasting of tongues as sharp as blades and flaunting a wealth of learning like a granary full of grain.

Upon reaching this point, one must be taught to remain in silent stillness; the path of speech is difficult to extend. All the words and phrases remembered from the past are merely counting another’s treasures.
Only then will you believe that this gate is extraordinary and is the special transmission outside the teachings.

Disciples of later generations, do not let yourselves be buried by your own negligence, lest you be ridiculed by others and bring disgrace upon the ancestral style. Do not say that because it does not require artificial cultivation, you have already attained something small.
This serves as a supplement. Since the branches are not understood, how can the root be clarified?
Not concerned with prosody and failing to comprehend the Way of Principle, one delights in composing songs and hymns.
The Ninth Treatise states: "The formats for songs and hymns in the School of the Lineage (Zongmen) are manifold; they may be short or long, modern or ancient, and employ borrowed tones."

They manifest through form and function; sometimes they employ concrete phenomena to extend their pedagogical intent, sometimes they discuss the ultimate truth in accordance with principle, and sometimes they subvert worldly affairs to correct popular customs.

Although their approaches differ, how can it be that their inspiration does not coincide? They collectively proclaim the causal conditions of the One Great Matter and together praise the samādhis of all Buddhas.
They rouse the later students and offer subtle critiques of former sages—all of which is intended to convey the central theme.

Regarding the literary style, how could one dare to compose recklessly? Yet, when observing the masters of various regions and the superior students who study under them, they treat song and verse as trivial matters and regard composition as a secondary concern.
They vent their feelings directly, mostly resembling the rambling talk of the wilds; they produce works at whim, which bear a striking resemblance to vulgar speech.
They consider themselves unconstrained by coarseness or filth, making no choice between the base and the refined, while claiming to emulate those who have transcended the mundane world.
These words proclaim the principle of returning to the foremost [truth]. Those with discernment read them and laugh in derision; the ignorant believe them and pass them along.
This causes the principles of names and reality to gradually vanish and the teachings of the Dharma-gate to become increasingly debased.

Have you not seen that the ten thousand verses of the *Avataṃsaka* and the thousands of ancestral hymns are all magnificent in their literary expression, entirely refined and pure without admixture? How could they be compared to these vulgar compositions that blend together in confusion?
Humor and jesting, when employed in later ages to compose scriptures, may be accepted as truth by the masses; yet even this requires an investigation of antiquity to ensure it is appropriate.
If one lacks natural talent, they should simply accept their own plainness; why must they insist on striving to emulate the brilliant and refined?

One who aspires to the worthy and wise should not present their own ugliness and clumsiness to disrupt the prevailing customs, nor weave together falsehoods and errors to bring about misfortune. Do not succumb to delusion and fabrication, thereby increasing future shame.
This is the tenth [point]:
Guarding One’s Own Shortcomings and Avoiding the Desire for Victory in Disputes.
The Commentary says: For instance, the monasteries throughout the land are extremely flourishing, and Zen communities are exceedingly numerous;
assemblies of no fewer than five hundred are common, and those with no Dharma at all are rare, numbering not even one or two.

Among them, there may occasionally be scholars who embrace the Way and persons of pure conduct who are willing to temporarily comply with the sentiments of the multitude and exert themselves to succeed to the patriarchal seat, gathering brothers from the ten directions to establish a single center.

At the site of enlightenment, he attended in the morning and participated in the evening assembly, never shrinking from toil or hardship. His purpose was to continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom and to guide those at the beginning stage of their practice;
it was not for the sake of seeking fame or reputation, nor out of greed for gain and offerings. Like a bell waiting to be struck, he responded when illness arose with medical care.

When he poured down the rain of Dharma, there was no partiality toward the great or the small; when he thundered the roar of Dharma, all far and near responded. Yet their flourishing or withering remained distinct, as did their movements.

To harbor discord and divergence is certainly not the sentiment of discernment; to employ the methods of acceptance and rejection is likely because one has merely waited for the wind of opportunity to succeed to the position and usurped the role of abbot, thereby claiming to have already attained the Supreme Vehicle and transcended worldly dharmas, while concealing one's own shortcomings.

They disparage the virtues of others; they deceive and delude the lowly and the simple; they exploit those who engage in slaughter and trade. They boast of their power and influence, and take pride in their rhetorical skill.

They mistake exposure and denunciation for compassion, and treat license and excess as virtuous conduct. They violate the prohibitions of the Buddha and cast aside the dignified decorum of the Saṃgha.

They even go so far as to insult and belittle those of the Two Vehicles and to perversely reject the Three Studies; how much more so when they fail to restrain themselves in matters of fundamental integrity?

They claim for themselves to be men of great attainment; yet, in this age of the semblance Dharma, when Māra is powerful and the Dharma is weak, they may don the monastic robes that have come down to them and usurp the sovereign grace and majesty of the king.
While their mouths discourse upon the causes of liberation, their hearts dally with the affairs of ghosts and spirits.
Having no sense of shame, how could one avoid transgressions? I now recount these matters in detail so that those who come after may be cautioned.

Encountering the conditions for Prajñā is no small matter; choosing the path of a teacher and disciple is especially difficult. Those who can maintain self-restraint will ultimately become great vessels.
I have forcefully administered this bitter medicine and am willing to accept slander and suspicion. May my fellow practitioners on the same path kindly assist in its propagation.
*The Ten Regulations for the School Gate* (End).
Postscript to the Reprint of the *Ten Regulations for the School Gate*.
The *Ten Guidelines for Discourse* (*Shiguilun*) was composed by Chan Master Fayan, the tenth-generation successor of Caoxi.

After the Chan Master personally encountered Dizang and received his instruction, every opening of his mouth and movement of his tongue was nothing other than resolving the entanglements and removing the fetters of others.
For instance, when a monk asked, "What is one drop of water from the Cao source? the answer was, "It is one drop of water from the Cao source.
Furthermore, when the monk Huichao asked, "What is the Buddha? the answer was, "You are Huichao.
To provide such instructions is like cooking iron to serve as rice or boiling wooden shavings for soup; it is intended to satisfy the hunger of all people in the world, yet it truly leaves them...
Since there is no place for lower teeth [to bite], how could one be willing to entangle others with the phrasing and meanings of literary compositions?
The composition of this treatise was intended, above all, to remedy the disease of the stammering and stifled silence among the masters of that time; it was undertaken as a matter of necessity.

Some may say that because the Master’s realization was stable and secret, and his knowledge and vision were vast and profound, he merely used this as a pretext to cast aside his own literary elegance and erudition.
The commentator is mistaken. In the year Wuyin (1236), the Librarian Yue of Nanping produced this text and once commissioned me to transcribe it.
It was carved onto printing blocks at the Jizhao Pagoda Cloister on Mount Jing. When Mount Jing suffered from the ravages of war and fire, the blocks were likewise consumed by the flames.
Now, the venerable Shōnin Min of Taisan’s Ue-uga has donated his own funds to reissue this work using an old manuscript he had previously transcribed, and has requested that I write a preface for it.
I have carefully examined the flawed editions of the past;
they were truly like the image seen by someone inside a jar at Xiakou, or the writing atop the beams at Langya—truly matters that rescue the world. Alas! From this day forward, when one reads...
If those who read this treatise are able to examine their own ailments, embody the intention of Master Tanyu, and are willing to take his excellent medicine, would that not be most excellent?
This colophon by Yuan Zhiyun, written while in Zhongzhou, was obtained from a collection in Korea and appended here.
